course.title: General Physics II Laboratory (Electricity and Magnetism)

coverage.notes: Every convention here comes from completed submissions plus one surviving blank handout, so this pack records what was submitted rather than what was required. That framing is now known to be too strong: an instructor turn-in specification DOES survive, on the last page of the archived blank handout, and it has not been mined. Until it is, treat every format rule below as observed practice that an instructor statement may override. No syllabus, rubric, graded return, or identifiable lab instructor was found in the student's iCloud term archive or his university OneDrive as of September 2026.

methods.title: Predict, build, test, compare
methods.when: Most items in the qualitative circuit labs (bulbs, series and parallel, switches).
steps: Draw the schematic with standard symbols, and a physical sketch when asked.
Write a prediction with its reasoning before building.
Build the circuit and record what is observed.
State whether the observation matched the prediction, and explain any mismatch in terms of current, voltage, or resistance.
pitfalls: Revising the prediction after the fact instead of recording the mismatch.
Proceeding past an instructor checkpoint without sign-off.

methods.title: Junction, loop, and power-balance checks
methods.when: DC resistor and bulb networks where currents, voltages, and powers are measured or simulated.
steps: Tabulate R, I, V, and P for every element with units.
Junction rule: the currents into each node sum to the currents out.
Loop rule: the drops around each loop sum to the source voltage.
Power balance: the source power equals the sum of element powers.
State each check with the numbers substituted, and name the size of any residual.
pitfalls: Treating a parallel pair as one element for the loop rule without saying so.
Rounding before checking, which hides or creates a residual.

methods.title: AC amplitude, RMS, and reactance from scope measurements
methods.when: The AC labs: signals and the oscilloscope, reactance and impedance, phasors, and RL/RC circuits.
steps: Record which quantity the instrument reports (amplitude, peak-to-peak, or RMS) and convert explicitly.
For a sinusoid, RMS equals the peak amplitude divided by the square root of 2.
Get an element's voltage from channel differences when it cannot be probed directly to ground.
Compute current from a known resistor's voltage, then reactance from the element's voltage divided by that current.
Plot reactance against frequency, with frequency on the horizontal axis, preferably on a log scale.
pitfalls: Mixing peak-to-peak and amplitude, which gives a factor-of-two error.
Swapping axes, or describing the plot's axes wrongly in the text.
Trusting the generator's dial instead of measuring the signal.

methods.title: RC and RL time constants
methods.when: Transient labs on RC and RL circuits.
steps: Write the charging or decay expression for the measured quantity.
Solve it for the time constant or the unknown element from a measured point, or fit it across several points.
Include every series resistance in the time constant, including the inductor's own winding resistance.
pitfalls: Omitting the source or winding resistance from the total resistance.

assignment_families.title: Weekly lab write-up
stages: in-lab work in pairs with instructor checkpoints
deliverables: a PDF write-up with a title block, numbered answers, tables and images, and an optional closing reflection
what_good_looks_like: Every handout item is answered, in order, labeled with its number, and none is skipped or left unfinished.
Each quantitative answer shows the relation used, the substituted values, and the result with units.
Each prediction item states the prediction and the reasoning, and then says whether the test confirmed it.
Tables and pasted images sit at the item that asks for them, and each is identified in a sentence.
Any reflection addresses the physics learned or a specific source of measurement error, in a professional register.
assignment_families.basis: Nine completed write-ups and one blank handout; the other handouts were not retained. The what_good_looks_like entries are inferred from the handout's own instructions and general lab practice, because no instructor rubric exists in the archive.
